There are two types of access control systems: Electric Strike and Magnetic Lock. These are the two methods used to automatically lock and unlock doors.

An Electric Strike means that if there’s a card reader outside, swiping a card triggers the security system to retract the strike, allowing the door to be pushed open. But what about a Magnetic Lock? This is essentially a magnet. Under normal circumstances, when locked, the metal plate (on the door) is held by the magnet (on the frame). As we know, when the magnet is energized, it becomes magnetic and holds the plate in place, locking the door. To open it, the magnet must be demagnetized by cutting power.

With Electric Strike, there’s a coordination aspect: if there’s a Push Bar (or Panic Bar) inside, pushing it can mechanically release the strike from within. However, this isn’t possible with Magnetic Lock because it requires power interruption to disengage. Even if there’s a Panic Bar behind it, pushing won’t open the door since the lock isn’t released.

Electric Strike is called Fail Secure, meaning: if power is lost, the door remains locked—unopenable from the outside with a card—but can still be opened from the inside using a handle or Panic Bar. Magnetic Lock is Fail Safe, allowing people to exit when power is cut.

In fire alarm system design, if the lock is an Electric Strike, it’s less of a concern because there are always internal mechanisms to open it. But if it’s a Magnetic Lock, the fire alarm system must control a relay to cut power, disabling the lock so the door can open.
